prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "INTEL CORP" (ticker INTC). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Intel fits few Rule Breaker traits: it is a 58-year-old incumbent that lost its technology lead to TSMC and share to AMD, not the top dog of an emerging industry. It does show strong price momentum (up about 179% in a year) and smart backers (the US government, NVIDIA and SoftBank), but its advantage is not clearly sustainable.
summaries.buffett: Intel is an understandable business with a famous brand, but its record is the opposite of consistent: revenue fell from $79.0B (2021) to $52.9B (2025), it suspended its dividend in 2024, it carries $50.5B of debt and free cash flow is negative because of heavy fab spending. Buffett would see a turnaround in a capital-intensive, fast-changing industry, not a durable compounder, and after the stock nearly tripled there is no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Inverting the problem shows many ways Intel could disappoint: the foundry may never win enough outside customers, AMD and Arm keep taking share, and the 2026 CPU shortage could reverse. Munger favored great businesses at fair prices; Intel is a hard turnaround now priced at about 5.9 times book value with GAAP losses.
summaries.lynch: Intel is a Lynch turnaround story (AI-driven CPU demand, 18A ramp, outside foundry customers) rather than a fast grower or stalwart. The CEO buying shares is a plus, but the share count jumped after the 2025 US government, NVIDIA and SoftBank deals, and with GAAP losses the P/E-to-growth test cannot be passed.
summaries.fisher: Intel meets some Fisher points (large R&D budget producing 18A and advanced packaging, management committed to new processes and products, a new CEO with deep technical knowledge), but it fails on long-run sales growth, profit margins and consistent R&D payoff after years of process delays. Fisher would want proof the foundry turnaround works.
summaries.graham: Intel fails Graham's defensive tests: it lost money in 2024 and 2025, suspended its dividend in 2024 after paying one since 1992, EPS has fallen over ten years, and it trades at about 5.9 times book value. Only its large size passes.
summaries.thiel: Intel is not a Zero to One company today: its technology is at best on par with TSMC and AMD rather than ten times better, and it competes in crowded markets. Its most unique asset is being the only US-based leading-edge chipmaker, a strategic position that could matter if geopolitics shifts demand away from Taiwan.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for AI-platform winners with improving profitability and disciplined spending; Intel benefits from AI-driven CPU demand and Lip-Bu Tan has cut costs hard, but foundry losses, negative free cash flow and heavy capex leave it far from his 'fit' standard.
summaries.druckenmiller: Intel fits Druckenmiller's interest in inflection points: revenue grew 25% in Q2 2026, non-GAAP EPS swung from -$0.10 to $0.42 and estimates are rising, with the stock up about 179% in a year. The open question is whether 2026's shortage-driven boom lasts beyond 18-24 months.
summaries.smith: Intel fails Terry Smith's good-company tests: returns on capital have been low or negative since 2022, gross margin fell from 56.0% (2020) to 34.8% (2025) and free cash flow is negative. It is the type of capital-intensive turnaround Fundsmith avoids.
summaries.greenblatt: Intel ranks poorly on the Magic Formula: return on its huge fab capital base is low, and with operating losses in 2025 and an enterprise value near $539B its earnings yield is minimal.
summaries.akre: Only the management leg of Akre's stool is arguably improving under Lip-Bu Tan; the business has not been exceptional for years and reinvestment into fabs has earned poor returns so far. Akre would likely wait for evidence of durable returns on capital.
summaries.pabrai: Intel was a Dhandho-style setup in 2024-25 (a famous business in a fixable setback with government backing), but after the stock rose from about $36 to $101.50 the low-risk, high-uncertainty bargain is gone. The downside if the foundry fails is now large.
summaries.wood: Intel is not an ARK-style disruptor: it is an incumbent defending x86 against Arm and GPUs, though AI CPUs, AI PCs and Mobileye's autonomous driving touch ARK themes. Its costs are not falling fast enough to open big new demand on their own.
summaries.ackman: Intel is a large, well-known business but not the simple, predictable, free-cash-flow generative company Ackman seeks; it carries $50.5B of debt and heavy capex. A turnaround thesis with government support could interest an activist, but the current price leaves little discount to value.
summaries.sleep: Intel historically shared scale economics through falling cost per transistor, but its loss of manufacturing leadership broke that advantage, and it is now raising prices in a shortage rather than passing savings to customers. Its 10-20 year position depends on the uncertain foundry turnaround.
summaries.valentine: Valentine favored huge markets and painful problems: Intel addresses both (compute for AI and a non-Taiwan source of leading-edge chips), but it is a mature incumbent, not a startup creating a new market.

momentum.evidence: INTC rose from about $36.40 (mid-October 2025) to about $101.50 on Oct 14, 2026 (+179%) and about +126% since April 1, 2026, versus about +17% for SPY over the year.

g4.evidence: CEO Lip-Bu Tan (former Cadence CEO) leads it, and the US government (about 10% stake), NVIDIA ($5B investment) and SoftBank are shareholders.

g6.evidence: After nearly tripling, many analysts rate it Hold with targets near the price (e.g. Bernstein $110, Mizuho $114, Susquehanna $115) and some call it expensive, but it is not widely labelled wildly overvalued.

simple.evidence: Making and selling CPUs is understandable, but judging the 18A/14A process roadmap and foundry economics requires specialist knowledge.

b2.evidence: Revenue fell from $79.0B (2021) to $52.9B (2025) and the company lost money in 2024 and 2025.

integrity.evidence: Lip-Bu Tan has been candid about foundry risks (saying 14A could be dropped without customers) and bought about $25M of stock, but past management overpromised on process roadmaps and capital spending.

b6.evidence: Tan has cut empire-building projects (cancelling Germany and Poland fabs, slowing Ohio), but the foundry strategy still requires very large capital commitments.

roic.evidence: Operating income fell from $23.7B (2020) to a loss in 2025 on a fab-heavy asset base, and debt stands at $50.5B.

fcf.evidence: Adjusted free cash flow was -$8,419M in Q2 2026 and operating cash flow of $9.7B in 2025 did not cover capex.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings were spent on fabs that lost money, while revenue fell from $77.9B (2020) to $52.9B (2025) and equity declined to $87,542M at June 2026.

safety.evidence: At about $101.50, roughly 5.9 times book value with GAAP losses, the price is far above a conservative asset or earnings value.

fairprice.evidence: A market value of about $518B against FY2026 consensus revenue of $63.1B (about 8.2 times sales) is rich for a business with a 40% gross margin and negative free cash flow.

mu5.evidence: There are many failure paths: the foundry may not win outside customers, AMD and Arm keep taking share, and the 2026 CPU shortage could end.

reinvest.evidence: It has large reinvestment opportunities (foundry, 14A, packaging), but returns on its past fab investments have been poor.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear turnaround: Q2 2026 revenue grew 25% to $16.1B and gross margin recovered to 40.4% from 27.5%.

ly3.evidence: Trailing GAAP earnings are negative (Q2 2026 net loss of $11,033M, driven by a mark-to-market loss), so the P/E-to-growth test cannot be met.

runway.evidence: AI CPU demand, foundry customers and advanced packaging offer growth, with consensus expecting about 19% revenue growth in 2026, but core x86 markets are mature and losing share.

ly7.evidence: CEO Lip-Bu Tan bought about $25M of stock, but diluted shares rose from 4,280M (2024) to 4,530M (2025) and about 5,104M in Q2 2026 after government and partner share issues.

ly8.evidence: Intel is one of the most heavily traded and discussed US stocks, with over 40 covering analysts.

fi2.evidence: It keeps developing new processes and products: 18A with RibbonFET and PowerVia, 14A with High-NA EUV, Panther Lake, Xeon 6+ and the Crescent Island inference GPU.

fi3.evidence: R&D finally delivered 18A and competitive Panther Lake chips, but for years it produced delays (10nm, 7nm) and Gaudi AI chips failed to gain traction.

fi4.evidence: Its sales relationships with every PC maker are strong, but it has struggled to sell foundry services, with only about $112M of outside foundry revenue excluding Altera in Q2 2026.

longterm.evidence: Management keeps investing in leading-edge process technology and US fabs despite losses, a decade-long bet.

gr1.evidence: Intel had $52.9B of revenue in 2025 and a market value of about $518B.

gr4.evidence: Intel suspended its dividend from Q4 2024 after paying one since 1992.

eps10.evidence: GAAP EPS was negative in 2024 and 2025, well below the level of ten years earlier.

gr6.evidence: Average earnings over recent years are near zero or negative, so the price is far above 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: With negative trailing earnings and a price of about 5.9 times book value, the test fails.

th1.evidence: Intel 18A is roughly competitive with TSMC's N2, not ten times better, and AMD often matches or beats its CPUs.

timing.evidence: AI agents have created a CPU shortage that helps Intel in 2026, and geopolitical pressure favors US fabs, but AI spending still flows mainly to NVIDIA GPUs and TSMC.

th3.evidence: Intel is an incumbent defending a large mature market (x86 CPUs), not a company growing from dominance of a small niche.

team.evidence: Lip-Bu Tan has a strong record at Cadence, but the team is still proving it can turn Intel around.

th5.evidence: It has deep distribution with every major PC and server maker and the 'Intel Inside' channel.

durable.evidence: x86 and US fabs should still matter in 10-20 years, but Arm, custom chips and TSMC threaten its position.

th7.evidence: Its bet on being the West's non-Asian leading-edge foundry is distinctive, but competitors and customers clearly see the same opportunity.

trend.evidence: It benefits from AI-driven CPU demand (data center revenue up 59% in Q2 2026), but is not a leading beneficiary of AI accelerators.

dr1.evidence: Non-GAAP EPS swung from -$0.10 (Q2 2025) to $0.42 (Q2 2026), revenue grew 25%, and consensus 2026 revenue has risen to about $63.1B.

dr2.evidence: 18A volume ramp and possible 14A customers could improve results, but the CPU shortage that lifts prices could fade.

dr4.evidence: Government support and AI capex help, but $50.5B of debt and heavy capex make it sensitive to rates and the PC cycle.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include Q3 2026 results on Oct 29 (guided $15.8-16.8B revenue), 14A customer announcements and possible foundry deals with Apple or Musk's Terafab.

dr7.evidence: Execution risk in the foundry and negative free cash flow make it unsuitable for a high-conviction concentrated position.

gm.evidence: GAAP gross margin was 34.8% in 2025 and 40.4% in Q2 2026, far below its 56.0% in 2020 and peers like AMD.

fcfyield.evidence: Free cash flow is negative (adjusted FCF of -$8,419M in Q2 2026).

gb2.evidence: Intel had an operating loss in 2025 against an enterprise value of about $539B.

pa2.evidence: Its 2022-2025 slump looked like a fixable setback that is now reversing, but the share price already reflects much of the recovery.

pa4.evidence: After a near-tripling, a foundry failure or end of the CPU shortage could cause a large, lasting loss; the stock fell from $142.35 to $81.79 within months in mid-2026.

wo1.evidence: Intel sells AI CPUs and Mobileye autonomous-driving chips, but it is not a leader in AI accelerators.

wo2.evidence: Its manufacturing costs have been higher than TSMC's and it is raising prices in 2026 rather than cutting them.

wo3.evidence: It touches AI, autonomous driving (Mobileye) and robotics/physical AI, but none at a leading scale.

wo4.evidence: Its core markets are mature; only a large foundry success could multiply its addressable market.

ac3.evidence: It is exposed to the PC and server cycle, interest rates on $50.5B of debt, export controls and US government policy.

ns1.evidence: Intel lost its cost advantage to TSMC and is raising prices (server ASPs up about 48% in Q2 2026) rather than sharing scale savings.

ns4.evidence: If 18A/14A win outside customers its position could be stronger in 10-20 years, but that is far from certain.

va2.evidence: It solves large problems: compute for AI and PCs and a secure non-Asian source of leading-edge chips.
